abstract: How does artificial intelligence (AI) change the case for markets relative to central planning? Both market participants and planners use AI to forecast demand and costs and develop ideas for products and methods of production, marketing, and distribution. I compare expected consumer benefits from their chosen innovations, less implementation and evaluation costs, without and with AI. Both have access to the same forecasts, consumer responses, and public trial results. Market participants also use information from purchases and competing bids that planning procedures do not reproduce. With other evidence unchanged in quality, better shared forecasts help both groups, but help planners more in the model because they begin with less information. I represent AI as increasing the number of ideas both groups examine, keeping their average net value and the variation around that average unchanged. I derive limits on the extra market cost per idea and the accuracy of shared forecasts. Below both limits, examining more ideas increases the market advantage after costs despite planners catching up, even with an unchanged extra market cost per idea. Forecast accuracy beyond the threshold instead shifts the comparison toward planning. If the net welfare difference in other activities remains unchanged, these conditions also determine which arrangement gains more from AI. A separate extension examines lost innovation benefits and additional costs from political and bureaucratic objectives under planning. Under the derived conditions, AI strengthens the market case by expanding the ideas examined and increasing the payoff from market-generated knowledge in choosing which to pursue.
title: When does artificial intelligence strengthen the case for markets? Revisiting the socialist calculation debate

abstract: The importance of private equity for euro area firms is increasing, with annual growth rates in assets under management exceeding 10%. Private equity buyouts affect more than just the firms being acquired. Using comprehensive data for Belgium, this column shows that the sales volumes of suppliers grow faster when there is a higher proportion of business with customers backed by private equity. But this advantage is lost during downturns, as investors push for cost savings. Buyouts can also crowd out competitors that depend on the same suppliers. Finally, high leverage implies greater interest rate sensitivity, so private equity buyouts can intensify the transmission of monetary policy to target firms and beyond.

abstract: Debates about tariff evasion have focused on Chinese goods entering the US. This column examines the reverse flow and finds that China’s retaliatory tariffs on imports from the US also induced evasion, especially through the misreporting of US-origin goods as originating from other third countries. Trade data and customs enforcement cases help distinguish origin misreporting from genuine trade diversion. The estimates attribute about 35% of the tariff-induced reduction in recorded imports to underreporting, highlighting the need for stronger country-of-origin verification and showing how tariff evasion can make US–China decoupling appear greater than it actually is.
authors: Huijia Liu, Enze Xie, Linhui Yu, Miaojie Yu
